title: Ashcombe Rising Revisited
premise: When a drowned man washes up in Ashcombe wearing clothes stolen from Ines Coldharbour's own closet, the insurance investigator's photographic memory becomes both her greatest asset and her deepest liability—because she recognizes the victim as a man officially dead for twelve years, the same year she first came to town. As Ines digs into old case files, she realizes someone has been editing the town's records for over a decade, and that her own carefully constructed identity was built on a lie planted by whoever killed him. The killer, revealed to be the town archivist who raised Ines after finding her abandoned, has been curating Ashcombe's history to bury a decades-old wrongful death, and now needs Ines—the only living witness—to disappear before the inquest. Ines turns the tables by feeding the killer false memories through doctored files, exposing him at the trial's opening, and choosing to stay in Ashcombe not as an invisible filing clerk but as the town's new keeper of true records, surrounded by the found family she finally admits she has.
about_author: V. M. Galloway is the pen name of a former municipal records clerk who spent nine years cataloguing small-town archives across coastal England before turning to fiction. Galloway writes mysteries about people who know too much and say too little, drawing on a fascination with how paper remembers what people prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Tide Returns What It Takes
chapters.summary: Ines Coldharbour, POV. A body washes up below the sea wall wearing Ines's own missing grey coat and scarf. Her photographic memory catalogs every detail of the scene, but one detail unravels her: the dead man's face belongs to Thomas Reeve, declared drowned twelve years ago. Emotional beat: cold shock beneath practiced composure.

chapters.title: Alphabetical Order
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. She retreats to the insurance office and pulls every file touching Thomas Reeve, discovering the 2012 drowning report contradicts itself in three places—details only someone with her memory would catch. Detective Sergeant Marr questions her about the stolen clothes. Emotional beat: the comfort of filing versus the dread of what the files contain.

chapters.title: A Wardrobe With Witnesses
chapters.summary: DS Marr, POV. Marr investigates the theft from Ines's flat and finds no forced entry, meaning the thief had a key or Ines is lying. He notes her unnervingly precise recollections and wonders whether precision is innocence or performance. Emotional beat: professional suspicion hardening into personal curiosity.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Daughter
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Flashback woven with present: twelve years ago, town archivist Edmund Voss took in the orphaned Ines, teaching her that records are safer than people. Now Voss warns her gently to let the police handle the body. Emotional beat: gratitude shadowed by the first flicker of doubt about the man who raised her.

chapters.title: Dead Man, Live Account
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Following insurance anomalies, Ines finds Thomas Reeve's life policy was paid out in 2012—to a beneficiary whose signature matches Voss's handwriting exactly. Someone collected money for a man who apparently just died again. Emotional beat: vertigo as her foundation story cracks.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Nell Pryce, harbor pub owner and Ines's only friend, POV. Nell recalls the night Reeve 'drowned'—she saw his boat leave with two men aboard, not one. She's kept quiet for twelve years out of fear. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing like something long submerged.

chapters.title: Edited History
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. In the town archive, Ines discovers pages of the 2012 inquest subtly replaced—her photographic memory lets her compare against documents she read years ago. The edits all protect one narrative: that nothing happened on the water that night. Emotional beat: horror at realizing memory is the only uncorrupted record left.

chapters.title: The Second Witness
chapters.summary: DS Marr, POV. Marr locates Ruth Ellery, the inquest's other witness, now living under a changed name two towns over. She agrees to talk, then vanishes before he returns. Marr begins suspecting the case has a keeper, not just a killer. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing he may be hunted too.

chapters.title: Clothes Make the Corpse
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Forensics confirm the clothing worn by the corpse came from Ines's closet—and inside the coat lining she finds a key tag from the archive basement. The message is unmistakable: someone wants her to look there, or wants her blamed. Emotional beat: paranoia tightening into resolve.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Sundays
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Reconstructing Voss's kindnesses—every meal, every lesson, every warning—Ines tests each memory against evidence and finds his care always steered her away from the harbor, the water, the year 2012. Emotional beat: grief arriving ahead of certainty; loving someone and suspecting them at once.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary
chapters.summary: DS Marr, POV. Marr traces the 2012 payout to a shell account still active, funding, among other things, the archive's preservation society. He confronts Voss informally; Voss is serene, quoting record-keeping law. Marr leaves convinced the archivist is guilty of something, just not yet murder. Emotional beat: frustration against a wall of legitimacy.

chapters.title: Ruth Ellery's Last File
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Ines finds Ruth Ellery's hidden statement mailed to the archive years ago and never filed—a confession that she and Reeve witnessed a fatal accident covered up by powerful town families, and that Voss helped bury it to protect them. Emotional beat: the sick clarity of understanding why.

chapters.title: Housekeeping
chapters.summary: Voss, POV (first time). Voss reflects on his life's work: curating Ashcombe's story, protecting it from its own sins, raising Ines as both daughter and archive of the one night he failed to erase. He decides the inquest must not open. Emotional beat: chilling tenderness—he believes he is the hero.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Knowing Voss reads everything she touches, Ines plants a false file suggesting she's found proof implicating the harbor master instead, and announces she'll testify at the inquest. It's a trap built from his own methods. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into cold strategy.

chapters.title: The Night Ferry
chapters.summary: DS Marr, POV. Marr tails Voss on the night before the inquest and loses him near the old ferry slip—but finds fresh rope burns and Reeve's original logbook, water-damaged, hidden in a mooring post. The logbook names names. Emotional beat: triumph undercut by the realization Ines is alone with the danger.

chapters.title: Archive Basement
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Summoned by a forged note in Marr's name, Ines descends into the archive basement where Voss waits among the shelves. He explains, reasonably, lovingly, that some stories must be maintained, and that she—his finest creation—will be recorded as a runaway, another unsolved file. Emotional beat: terror held at bay by intellect.

chapters.title: Photographic Evidence
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Cornered, Ines fights the only way she can: with memory. She recites, verbatim, every document Voss ever altered, every contradiction, forcing him to confront that his curated history exists only because she never forgot it. His composure fractures. Emotional beat: the quiet weapon of perfect recall turned lethal.

chapters.title: The Inquest Opens
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs—Marr, Nell, Ines. At the inquest's opening session, Ines takes the stand and, rather than flee as Voss planned, presents the logbook, the payout trail, and her testimony. Voss, seated in the gallery, understands the trap has closed. Emotional beat: public reckoning; the town holding its breath.

chapters.title: Confession in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Voss, POV. Rather than run, Voss returns to the archive to burn the remaining originals—erasure as final act. Ines and Marr arrive; Voss surrenders the matches but not the argument, telling Ines that forgetting is mercy. She answers that remembering is justice. Emotional beat: tragic symmetry between mentor and student.

chapters.title: Sentencing the Silence
chapters.summary: DS Marr, POV. Voss is charged; the town's powerful families scramble as the logbook's names surface. Marr closes the file on Reeve's death and opens a dozen others. Nell finally tells her whole story on record. Emotional beat: exhausted relief; the machinery of lawful justice grinding awake at last.

chapters.title: Found Family, Filed Properly
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Weeks later, Ines sorts the recovered archive, deciding which lies to preserve as history and which truths to restore. Nell, Marr, and Ruth Ellery—returned and safe—gather in the pub. Ines accepts, aloud, that they are hers and she is theirs. Emotional beat: warmth earned through wreckage.

chapters.title: Ashcombe Rising
chapters.summary: Ines, POV. Offered a better job elsewhere, Ines declines, accepting appointment as the town's new custodian of records. On the sea wall she scatters flowers for Thomas Reeve and writes the first entry of a new, honest ledger. Emotional beat: an ending that is also a beginning—identity chosen, not assigned.
